analysis.one_liner: Extends minimum wage and overtime protections to home care workers, who are currently exempt.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 with 83 cosponsors, all Democrats, and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Home care workers — home health aides and personal care aides who care for elderly and disabled people in their homes — are carved out of federal minimum wage and overtime rules under a Depression-era exemption meant for casual babysitters. This bill narrows that exemption to actual casual babysitting and repeals the separate exemption for companionship services, so home care workers would earn at least the federal minimum wage and time-and-a-half pay for hours over 40 a week.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly two million home care workers, most of them women and disproportionately immigrants and women of color, whose work has been excluded from basic wage and overtime protections. They would be guaranteed the federal minimum wage ($7.25 an hour, or more in many states) and overtime pay beyond 40 hours a week. Workers who now routinely put in 50- or 60-hour weeks without overtime pay would see direct raises in their paychecks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Home health and personal care aides

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the exemption in Section 13(b)(21) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, which excludes 'companionship services' workers — the category home care workers fall into — from minimum wage and overtime requirements [S2].

Narrows the remaining exemption for domestic workers so it applies only to casual babysitting of children in the child's own home, and explicitly defines babysitting to exclude trained home care workers, home health aides, and personal care aides [S2].

Home care workers who regularly work long shifts, including live-in and overnight arrangements common in this field, would become entitled to overtime pay at one and a half times their regular rate for hours beyond 40 a week [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Home care agencies that employ aides, and the payers behind them — state and federal Medicaid programs, which fund most paid home care, and families who pay for care out of pocket. Rising labor costs would flow into agency reimbursement rates, government budgets, or private pay rates. Some agencies might respond by cutting scheduled hours, which could make care harder to arrange for some families.
analysis.who_pays_short: Home care agencies, Medicaid, private-pay families

drawbacks.text: Higher labor costs for agencies would have to be paid by someone: states and the federal government would face higher Medicaid costs unless reimbursement rates rise, and families paying privately would pay more per hour of care [S2].

Agencies facing higher wage bills could respond by trimming scheduled hours, consolidating visits, or shifting more care to unpaid family members, which could leave some families with gaps in care [S2].

The bill sets the floor at the existing federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour, which is below living wages in most of the country; it guarantees a legal minimum but does not by itself make home care work pay well [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and direct: a large, historically underpaid, largely female workforce gains minimum wage and overtime rights it has been denied for decades. The costs are real too — someone must pay for the hours, and because Medicaid dominates home care funding, the money would mostly come from public budgets and private-pay families. The bill is a clean extension of existing wage law rather than a new funding mechanism, so its practical effect depends on whether Medicaid rates follow. On balance it addresses a well-documented gap in wage law for workers who are among the lowest-paid in the country.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 12, 2026 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, joined by 82 other House members as original cosponsors [S1][S4].
All 83 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce on the day it was introduced, and the public record shows no further action since [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill stalled in committee, home care agencies keep operating under the current exemption and owe no overtime or minimum wage under federal law; workers gain nothing yet. No final beneficiary is determined while the bill is pending.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Home care agencies, under the current rules

for.name: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 82 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 83 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including members such as Rashida Tlaib, Pramila Jayapal, Katherine Clark allies on labor issues, Joe Courtney-era labor committee members like Mark Takano and Suzanne Bonamici, and Frank Pallone allies; all 83 are Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the 83 cosponsors is a Democrat and no Republican has signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority and controlling the Education and Workforce Committee, the bill has advanced no further [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Home care and home health agencies
industries.note: These agencies employ most home care aides and have relied on the federal exemption to avoid paying minimum wage and overtime; the bill removes that shield and raises their labor bill. The added cost would show up in what families and Medicaid pay, so the agencies' interest in keeping the exemption runs against the workers' interest in higher pay.

Most paid home care is funded through Medicaid, so guaranteeing minimum wage and overtime would raise program costs unless reimbursement rates rise. Paying aides properly is also what keeps home care staffed and keeps people out of costlier nursing homes.
Households that hire aides with their own money would face higher hourly costs, though for direct casual babysitters the exemption remains intact under the bill's narrow definition.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Education and Workforce Committee, which is controlled by the Republican majority, with no Republican cosponsors, no scheduled hearing, and no scheduled markup. In this Congress it is very unlikely to reach the House floor; the realistic path is that it stays in committee unless something changes — a discharge petition, a leadership decision, or a shift after the 2026 elections.
